headline: Private credit exposed to residential construction faces significant pain — fund managers tightening redemptions signals stress ahead
reasoning: Esho notes that much of the rapid growth in private credit has flowed into residential construction because fees were higher and banks had stepped back from that space. He sees this as very problematic. Signs include fund managers tightening redemptions, which he reads as a signal of coming pain. He describes the sector as undergoing an industry washout after rapid growth.
quote: It depends on the underlying asset class and the type of private credit exposure. You know, private credit is a term that encompasses a lot of different types of lending and a lot of different types of assets. And unfortunately, a lot of that growth has been in construction, residential construction. Because the fees were greater, the banks had stepped stepped out of that space more prominently. And so it sucked in a lot of that private capital fund flow. And that's going to be very problematic. I think if you have a listen to some of the commentary coming out, if you have a look at the and see the ways that fund managers of these private credit funds have tightened redemptions, it does suggest that there's going to be pain away from construction, particularly residential construction.

sector: Commercial Real Estate — large format retail, data centres
headline: Conviction building around large-format retail and data centres — strong income streams and inflation hedges make them resilient even if rates rise further
reasoning: Esho expects continued conviction around assets with strong income streams such as large format retail and data centres. These assets tend to have good pricing power and inflation hedges built in, meaning they can weather a higher-rate environment better than more opportunistic commercial plays.
quote: I think what you'll continue to see is more conviction around around large format retail, around data centers, around the assets where the income stream is strong. Even if rates do rise, they tend to have good pricing pressure. They have inflation hedges built into them.

headline: Australian property must be viewed in global context — rising rates across developed markets are pressuring yields and cap rates, with divergent outcomes by segment
reasoning: Peter Esho argues that Australia is not immune from the global interest rate cycle that is changing. Rising rates are putting pressure on yields and cap rates broadly. More expensive, premium and discretionary property markets are falling harder, while the affordable end of the residential market is holding up supported by natural demand and government policy.
quote: I think what's really important is that a lot of the time we view the Australian property market in our own bubble, but we should also view it in an overall context, global context. And rates are starting to rise all across the board in most developed markets, and Australia is not immune from that. So we are in an interest rate cycle that's changed and changing. And because of that, there's going to be a lot of pressure on yields and on cap rates. And so we're seeing different markets behave differently. Obviously markets that are more expensive, the more premium markets the more discretionary markets are coming off more. The affordable end of the residential market is holding up pretty well. That's supported not only by natural demand but also by government policy.

headline: Entry-level and affordable residential to hold up due to structural undersupply, rising rents, and lower replacement costs, even with further rate hikes
reasoning: Esho notes that building starts and approvals were ticking up but large residential developer collapses and weak investor sentiment are weighing on supply, meaning undersupply is likely to worsen over the next year or two. Rising rents and lower prices support the bottom end of the market. He sees middle and entry-level housing as still quite attractive, with rents rising because housing is still in demand.
quote: There is a natural undersupply in the market. The natural supply undersupply is probably going to get worse over the next year or two. If we have a look at building starts and approvals, they were ticking up. But you know when you have large residential developers collapsing, you have sentiment away from residential investment that does impact supply. And so because of that supply, I think the bottom end or the entry level of the market is going to be is going to hold up relatively okay. You also have rising yields. You know, rents are increasing. Prices have come down. And so that's going to support the market.

headline: Bullish on entry-level and mid-market residential housing: undersupply, rising rents and high replacement costs provide a floor even as developers struggle to bring residual stock to market
reasoning: Peter Esho argues that residential housing, particularly at the entry and middle price levels, remains attractive because supply is not surging the way it typically does at market tops. Rents are rising precisely because demand for housing is intact, and the cost of replacing residential stock continues to climb rather than fall. Developers are struggling with funding constraints in private credit markets and challenging build conditions, which suppresses new supply. Without that oversupply dynamic, Esho believes there is limited risk of a housing collapse, giving him comfort in the segment.
quote: I think those parts of the market are still going to stay strong. That's why rents are rising. Rents are rising because housing is still in demand. You usually have a housing collapse when you have a lot of supply coming on to the market. When the market gets wobbly this time, that's not happening. You've got funding issues in private credit development has become a very difficult business. Building is very challenging, but you don't have that supply that you tend to get at the top of the market. And so that gives me a lot of comfort there.

headline: Private credit industry is maturing and washing out; better risk frameworks expected after the cycle, with growth areas still requiring private capital
reasoning: Esho sees the private credit industry broadly going through a washout after rapid growth, but believes this will lead to better mandates and improved risk management. He draws a parallel to how banks managed their balance sheets during 2008-09 and the European debt crisis. Growth areas will continue to require private capital and there will be opportunities once risk is priced more appropriately.
quote: This is really, I think, a maturing of an industry that has grown rapidly is now going to go through a washout. But there will be better, you know, there'll be better mandates, more, um, better risk measures in place. And I think the best investors can learn from the way that the banks manage their balance sheets. During 2008 2009 around the European debt crises. Um, you know, if you have a look at and see how the banks managed, you'll see similar types of management arrangements coming in so that the next wave can price risk more appropriately.

headline: Premium and discretionary residential segments will remain challenged until the interest rate cycle turns
reasoning: Esho is explicit that more discretionary parts of the residential market will remain challenged until either the interest rate cycle changes or forward-looking rates start to come down. There is no near-term catalyst identified for a recovery in this segment.
quote: The more discretionary parts of the market are going to, you know, really remain challenged until the interest rate cycle changes or something happens where there's, you know, forward looking rates coming down.

headline: Opportunistic commercial plays, particularly office and development, face a tough outlook
reasoning: Esho singles out office and development-focused commercial players as segments that will find conditions tough in the current rate environment. The lack of inflation hedges and weaker income streams make these sectors vulnerable.
quote: Where the struggle will be is on the more opportunistic commercial players, particularly around office or development. Those sectors are going to find it tough.

headline: Larger and institutional investors are moving into data centres, AI infrastructure and evolving power-grid assets as structural demand from a changing world accelerates
reasoning: Esho notes that larger and institutional investors are increasingly looking towards data centres, AI-related infrastructure, and new power-grid assets. He frames this as a structural shift driven by the changing nature of the global economy and technology adoption, suggesting these asset classes are attracting significant capital flows from sophisticated investors.
quote: The areas that we focus on, larger investors, institutional investors are looking forward into the data centre space, into AI, into, um, you know, the way that the power grid is changing all those different types of assets that are starting to emerge because the world is changing.
